newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ's Apple Fields threatens closure.
newsitem.headline: NZ's Apple Fields threatens closure.

text.p: Listed orchardist Apple Fields said on Wednesday it would close all its orchards at the end of the month unless it was granted an export licence for a proposed new joint venture.
If it is not allowed to export its total crop through the planned joint venture deal, Apple Fields would become a property development and investment company.
The orchards' closure would mean the loss of over 2000 full and part-time jobs in Christchurch and the loss of over NZ$20 million annually to the Christchurch economy.
Apple Fields has told the Apple and Pear Marketing Board its application to export its entire apple crop this season is on an "all-or-nothing" basis.

Apple Fields said the major joint venture, with four leading fruit distributors in the United States, Europe and Asia, would integrate the total process from orchard to final distribution, through a variety of brands, to supermarkets throughout the northern hemisphere.
It said the joint venture was budgeted to earn NZ$28.5 million for Apple Fields, compared with a maximum of NZ$15.2 million that would be paid by ENZA for the same crop.
The application is expected to be heard by the marketing board next week.
Apple Fields has applied for export licences in the past, but its main applications have been rejected.

Chairman Murray Valentine said the closure would represent a commercial tragedy, with the needless loss of skilled staff, productive horticultural assets, international marketing structures and innovative food branding.

"The Apple Fields board has confidence in the long-term viability of the apple industry if it was allowed to export its own product, through its own international marketing and partnerships," he said.
However, it was demonstrably clear that the marketing board could not provide a commercially viable return, given its very high cost structures and its limited market strategies, Valentine said.

He said realistically Apple Fields could not have confidence its application would be fairly considered. If it were rejected, the orcharding operations would close and Apple Fields would pursue legal remedies for damages against both the Apple and Pear Marketing Board and the government.
Valentine said the joint venture would grow the total New Zealand apple export market, because none of the partners was currently sourcing New Zealand fruit.
All fruit would be marketed through established brands, rather than as New Zealand sourced produce, therefore avoiding any market conflict.
It would not conflict with or interrupt the Apple and Pear Board's own export activities, Valentine said.
